n: The Athanasian Creed is not a conciliar text, but it was received in the Latin liturgy as a rule of faith; its doctrine of the Trinity and the Incarnation is of faith.
The creed of the first ecumenical council; its confession that the Son is of one substance with the Father is defined dogma.
The anathemas of Pope Damasus's Roman synod (382); widely received as a statement of faith, though not an ecumenical definition.
The creed of Constantinople I, received at Chalcedon; defined dogma, including the divinity of the Holy Spirit.
Canons of an African council, confirmed by Pope Zosimus and received by the whole Church against Pelagius. Their teaching on the necessity of grace was later defined at Trent.
Cyril's second letter to Nestorius, read and approved at Ephesus as agreeing with Nicaea: the hypostatic union and Mary as Mother of God.
Cyril's twelve anathemas were read at Ephesus; whether the council formally adopted them is debated. Constantinople II later endorsed their doctrine.
The Indiculus on grace, compiled about 435–442 (probably by Prosper of Aquitaine) from papal and African statements; later treated as an authoritative papal summary against Semipelagianism.
Leo the Great's Tome, acclaimed at Chalcedon; its doctrine was taken into the council's definition.
The definition of Chalcedon: one person in two natures. Defined dogma.
Canons of the regional Council of Orange (529), confirmed by Boniface II (n. 200a). Received as binding against Semipelagianism; their core was later taken up by Trent.
Boniface II's letter confirming Orange II.
Anathemas of Constantinople II. The Christological canons are defined dogma; the condemnation of the Three Chapters is a judgment on particular persons and writings.
The definition of Constantinople III: two natural wills and operations in Christ. Defined dogma.
The definition of Nicaea II on the veneration of images. Defined dogma.
Lateran IV's profession Firmiter: the Trinity, creation, the Incarnation, the one Church and transubstantiation. Defined dogma.
Lateran IV's condemnation of Abbot Joachim's account of the divine unity, with an explicit refusal to condemn his monastery or person.
The precept of annual confession and Easter Communion is Church law. That mortal sins must be confessed is divine law, as Trent teaches (n. 916).
Lyons II defines that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle and one spiration.
The profession of faith required of Emperor Michael Palaeologus and accepted at Lyons II.
Unam Sanctam. Only its final sentence, on the necessity of subjection to the Roman Pontiff for salvation, is generally held to be the definition; the argument from the two swords is not.
The Council of Vienne: the rational soul is of itself and essentially the form of the body. Defined dogma.
John XXII's bull against Eckhart: seventeen articles condemned as heretical, eleven as evil-sounding, rash and suspect of heresy (n. 529).
Benedictus Deus: the immediate vision of God for the purified and immediate punishment for those dying in mortal sin. A papal definition.
Wycliffe's 45 articles, condemned at Constance and by Martin V with graded censures.
Constance defends Communion under one kind as a lawful custom and condemns calling it sacrilegious; the practice itself is discipline, which later councils adjusted.
Hus's 30 articles, condemned at Constance.
Florence's decree of union with the Greeks: the procession of the Spirit, the Eucharist, the last things and the primacy. Defined dogma.
The Decree for the Armenians, an instruction on the sacraments. Not every statement is a definition: Pius XII settled the matter of ordination differently (n. 2301).
Florence's decree for the Jacobites: the Trinity, the canon, and the necessity of the Church. Its statement on salvation is read with Pius IX on invincible ignorance (n. 1677).
Lateran V: the individual human soul is immortal and is the form of the body. Defined dogma.
Leo X's Exsurge Domine against Luther: 41 propositions condemned respectively, without assigning a censure to each (n. 781).
Trent receives the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed as the foundation of its work.
Trent on Scripture and Tradition and the canon of Scripture, with an anathema. Defined dogma.
The Vulgate declared authentic for public use: a juridical judgment about the Latin text, not a critical one (compare Pius XII, n. 2292).
The rule that Scripture is not to be interpreted against the sense of the Church or the consent of the Fathers.
Trent's decree on original sin. Defined dogma; it deliberately leaves Mary out of its scope (n. 792).
The doctrinal chapters of the decree on justification. Authoritative, and much of their content is of faith, but the defining texts are the canons that follow.
Trent's 33 canons on justification. Defined dogma.
Trent's canons on the sacraments in general, baptism and confirmation. Defined dogma.
The doctrinal chapters on the Eucharist; the corresponding canons (n. 883–893) are the definitions.
Trent's canons on the Eucharist, including transubstantiation (n. 884). Defined dogma.
The doctrinal chapters on penance; the canons (n. 911–925) are the definitions.
Trent's canons on penance and on the anointing of the sick. Defined dogma.
Trent's teaching on Communion under both kinds and of children.
Trent's canons: Christ is received whole under one kind, and Communion under both is not required of all by divine law.
The doctrinal chapters on the sacrifice of the Mass; the canons (n. 948–956) are the definitions.
Trent's canons on the sacrifice of the Mass. Defined dogma; canon 9 (n. 956) concerns the Church's authority over rites and language.
The doctrinal chapters on holy orders.
Trent's canons on holy orders. Defined dogma.
The doctrinal chapters on matrimony.
Trent's canons on matrimony. Canon 7 (n. 977) is worded to defend the Church's teaching without condemning Eastern practice directly.
Trent's decree on purgatory. Defined dogma.
Trent on the invocation of saints, relics and images: their veneration is good and useful. The instructions against abuses are discipline.
Trent: the Church has the power to grant indulgences, and their use is salutary.
Tametsi: clandestine marriages declared invalid for the future. Church law on the form of marriage.
Pius V's condemnation of Baius, respectively and in the sense intended by their authors; the bull grants that some could be maintained in some sense (n. 1080).
Innocent X's Cum occasione: Jansen's five propositions, each condemned as heretical among other censures.
Alexander VII: the five propositions are in Jansen's book and condemned in his sense. A dogmatic fact, held definitively.
Innocent XI's condemnation of Molinos's quietism, with graded censures applied respectively (n. 1288).
Innocent XII's condemnation of Fénelon's propositions on pure love, in their obvious sense (n. 1349); Fénelon submitted.
Clement XI's Unigenitus: 101 propositions of Quesnel condemned in globo with censures applied respectively.
Benedict XIV's Vix pervenit on usury. Its principle stands; its application changed with the economy (see the disputed question).
Pius VI's Auctorem fidei against the Synod of Pistoia. Each proposition carries its own censure, often conditional on a stated sense.
The Immaculate Conception, defined by Pius IX in 1854.
Quanta Cura. Some theologians held it to be ex cathedra; others treat it as authoritative teaching. Its relation to Dignitatis Humanae is a disputed question.
The Syllabus of Errors. Each proposition is condemned in the sense of the document it is drawn from; theologians differ on the binding force of the Syllabus as a collection.
The doctrinal chapters of Vatican I's Dei Filius. Authoritative; the canons that follow are the definitions.
Vatican I's canons on God, revelation, faith and reason. Defined dogma.
The preface and first chapter of Pastor Aeternus.
Canon: Peter received a true primacy of jurisdiction from Christ.
Chapter 2 of Pastor Aeternus.
Canon: Peter has perpetual successors in the primacy, the Roman Pontiffs.
Chapter 3 of Pastor Aeternus; the canon that follows is the definition.
Canon: the Pope's jurisdiction is full, supreme, ordinary and immediate over all the faithful.
Chapter 4 of Pastor Aeternus, the historical and theological case for infallibility.
The definition of papal infallibility and its canon.
The forty propositions drawn from Rosmini. In 2001 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith judged the concerns superseded when read within his own system.
Leo XIII's judgment that Anglican orders are invalid, listed in 1998 among truths to be held definitively.
Lamentabili: 65 Modernist propositions condemned by the Holy Office and approved by Pius X.
The Oath against Modernism, required of clergy from 1910 until 1967.
Casti Connubii on contraception. Authoritative teaching, repeated in Humanae Vitae; some theologians hold it is also infallible by the ordinary universal magisterium.
The Assumption, defined by Pius XII in 1950.
Early forms of the creed and related formulas, collected by the editors as witnesses to the baptismal faith.
The creed of the councils of Toledo (400, revised 447) with its anathemas against the Priscillianists; a regional profession, widely received.
Clement of Rome's letter to Corinth: the earliest witness to Roman intervention in another church, not a decree.
Reports by Hippolytus and Tertullian, both hostile witnesses, of the teaching and decisions of popes Zephyrinus and Callistus.
Letters of Pope Cornelius on the unity of the episcopate and the Roman clergy.
Pope Stephen's rule that those baptized by heretics are not rebaptized; later confirmed by Arles, Nicaea and Trent (n. 860).
Pope Dionysius against tritheism and Sabellianism, a precursor of Nicaea.
Canons of the regional Council of Elvira: early Spanish discipline on marriage, clerical continence and baptism.
The Council of Arles (314) against rebaptizing those baptized by heretics in the name of the Trinity.
Disciplinary canons of Nicaea on receiving heretics and on viaticum for the dying.
Pope Julius I on referring disputed cases to Rome.
Canons of the Western Council of Serdica on appeals to the bishop of Rome; later sometimes cited as Nicene.
The Roman synod under Damasus on the Holy Spirit and the canon of Scripture (part of the later Decretum Gelasianum tradition); the canon was later defined at Trent (n. 783–784).
Constantinople I's first canon: the Nicene faith confirmed and the heresies of the time anathematized.
Siricius's decretal to Himerius, the first surviving papal decretal: Peter bears the burdens of all in his successor.
Siricius: Arians are received by the laying on of hands, not rebaptized.
Siricius on betrothal and the marriage blessing.
Siricius on the continence of the higher clergy and the ordination of monks.
Siricius defends Mary's perpetual virginity, which the Church holds as of faith.
The African canon of Scripture; later defined at Trent (n. 783–784).
Anastasius I names Liberius among the confessors for the Nicene faith.
Decretals of Innocent I on baptism, reconciliation of the dying, the canon, confirmation, anointing of the sick and the authority of the Apostolic See.
Zosimus: the authority of the Apostolic See, and his Tractoria against Pelagius on original sin.
Boniface I on the finality of Rome's judgments; Celestine I on penance for the dying.
The speech of the papal legate at Ephesus, recorded in its acts; not a decree of the council. Vatican I cites it (n. 1824).
Ephesus forbids composing a creed other than that of Nicaea.
Ephesus confirms the condemnation of the followers of Celestius and Nestorius.
Celestine I commends the authority of Augustine.
An editorial cross-reference.
Leo the Great: sins are confessed secretly to priests; public reading of them is forbidden.
Leo the Great on the sacrament of penance.
Chalcedon's letter to Pope Leo, acknowledging him as head of the council.
Chalcedon's disciplinary canons on ordinations and the clergy.
Simplicius on guarding the faith handed down and the unchangeableness of doctrine.
The retraction required of the priest Lucidus at Arles (475) on grace and predestination.
Gelasius: what has been condemned is not to be reopened.
An editorial cross-reference.
The Decretum Gelasianum's canon. Its attribution to Gelasius is doubtful (it is probably a sixth-century compilation); its canon agrees with later definitions.
Gelasius on the Roman see and the patriarchal sees, and on the authority of councils and Fathers.
The Decretum Gelasianum's list of books not received; attribution doubtful.
Gelasius on the remission of sins and the two natures of Christ.
Anastasius II on the validity of ordinations by schismatics and on the origin of souls.
The Formula of Hormisdas (519), signed by the Eastern bishops to end the Acacian schism; cited by Vatican I for the infallibility of the Roman see (n. 1833).
Hormisdas on the canon, the primacy, the councils and the authority of Augustine.
Orange II on original sin and grace (see n. 174–199).
John II approves the formula that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh, and confesses Mary as Mother of God.

Anathemas against Origenism from the synod of Constantinople (543), accepted by Pope Vigilius; whether Constantinople II adopted them is debated. Their teaching that the punishment of the damned has no end is of faith.
Constantinople II confesses the faith of the four previous councils.
The closing of Constantinople II's anathemas.
Pelagius I's profession of faith on the last things.
Pelagius I on the form of baptism and the primacy.
Anathemas of the regional Council of Braga (561) against Priscillianism.
Pelagius II on the unity of the Church and the necessity of union with it.
Gregory the Great on Christ's knowledge (against the Agnoetae), on the baptism and orders of heretics, and on the moment of the hypostatic union.
Honorius I's letters to Sergius, later condemned at Constantinople III; whether they taught monothelitism or only spoke loosely is a historical question.
John IV's defense of the sense of Honorius's words.
The canons of the Lateran Synod of 649 under Martin I against monothelitism. Received by Constantinople III; their doctrine, including Mary's perpetual virginity (n. 256), is held as of faith.
The creed of Toledo XI (675): a regional profession, long esteemed as an exact statement of Trinitarian and Christological doctrine.
Pope Agatho's Roman council (680) on the hypostatic union, sent to Constantinople III.
Toledo XV's defense of its Trinitarian and Christological formulas.
The profession of faith of Toledo XVI.
Gregory II, Gregory III and Zachary on the form and minister of baptism and on confirmation.
Hadrian I on the primacy, against Adoptionism, and against abuses in Spain.
Disciplinary canons of Nicaea II.
Hadrian I against the Adoptionists.
The regional councils of Frankfurt (794) and Friuli (796) against Adoptionism.
The Council of Pavia (850) on the anointing of the sick.
The regional councils of Quiersy (853) and Valence (855) on predestination and grace. They differ in emphasis and were not ratified as definitions.
Roman councils and letters of Nicholas I on the primacy, the freedom of the Church, marriage and baptism.

Canons of Constantinople IV (869–870), counted in the West as the eighth ecumenical council: canon 3 on images and canon 11 on the one rational soul (n. 338) are doctrinal; others concern church order.
The canonization of Ulrich of Augsburg (993), the first known papal canonization.
The profession of faith of Leo IX (1053).
Leo IX on the primacy, and the Roman council on ordinations by simoniacs.
The oath imposed on Berengarius (1079): the bread and wine are substantially changed into Christ's body and blood.
Regional councils on the diaconate, obedience to the Church, and ordinations by heretics and simoniacs.
Canons of Lateran I and II on simony, celibacy, investiture and usury; Lateran II's canon against those who reject the sacraments (n. 367) is doctrinal.
The errors of Peter Abelard, condemned at Sens and by Innocent II (1140 or 1141).
Innocent III's reply: an unbaptized priest who died confessing the faith attained heaven by the baptism of desire.
The profession at Rheims (1148) against Gilbert de la Porrée on the Trinity.
Alexander III condemns the proposition that Christ as man is not something (Christological nihilism).
Alexander III on contracts, the bond of marriage and the form of baptism.
Lateran III on simony and against heretics.
The Council of Verona (1184) on the sacraments, against the Cathars.
Decretals of Urban III and Innocent III on usury, marriage, the Pauline privilege, baptism, the Eucharist and confirmation.
The profession of faith prescribed by Innocent III for returning Waldensians, including n. 425 on civil power.
Lateran IV's decrees against heretics, on the Greeks, the patriarchs, good faith in prescription and relics; mostly church law.
Decretals of Honorius III and Gregory IX on the sacraments and usury, and Gregory IX on keeping to the tradition of theological language.
Innocent IV's letter to the Greeks (1254), tolerating their rites and teaching on purgatory and hell (n. 456–457).
Alexander IV condemns William of St. Amour's attack on the mendicant orders.
Boniface VIII on the jubilee indulgence, and the opening of Unam Sanctam (its final sentence, n. 469, is the definition).
Benedict XI on repeating confession of sins already absolved.
The Council of Vienne condemns eight errors of the Beghards and Beguines.
Vienne: whoever obstinately holds that usury is no sin is to be punished as a heretic.
Vienne: one baptism regenerating all who are baptized is to be confessed by all.
Vienne calls the view that grace and virtues are infused in baptized infants the more probable opinion, without defining it.
John XXII condemns errors of the Fraticelli and of John of Pouilly.
John XXII to the Armenians on hell and the punishment of original sin.
John XXII's Cum inter nonnullos (1323): the assertion that Christ and the apostles owned nothing at all is declared heretical.
Benedict XII's list of errors attributed to the Armenians.
Clement VI's Unigenitus (1343) on the treasury of the Church and indulgences.
Clement VI's condemnation of Nicholas of Autrecourt's philosophical theses.
Clement VI's questions to the Armenians on the primacy, purgatory and confirmation.
Urban V and Gregory XI condemn errors on poverty and on the Eucharist.
Martin V's questions for suspected Wycliffites and Hussites (Inter Cunctas, 1418), approved with the council's condemnations.
Constance condemns as heretical Jean Petit's thesis that any tyrant may be killed by any subject.
Florence's note that the Roman Church's form of consecration is the words of Christ.
Callistus III approves the rent contract (census) as lawful.
Pius II's Execrabilis: appeals from the pope to a future council are forbidden under excommunication.
Pius II condemns the errors of Zanini de Solcia.
Pius II forbids Franciscans and Dominicans to call each other heretics over Christ's blood during the three days; the question is left open.
Sixtus IV condemns errors of Peter de Rivo (future contingents) and Peter de Osma (penance).
Sixtus IV on indulgences for the dead, applied by way of suffrage.
Sixtus IV approves the feast of the Immaculate Conception and forbids each side to call the other heretical; the question is left open until 1854.
Lateran V judges the Mountains of Piety, with their modest charges, not usurious.
Lateran V's Pastor Aeternus (1516): the pope alone convokes, transfers and dissolves councils; Basel's later acts have no weight.
Leo X on the doctrine of indulgences (1518).
Pius IV on clandestine marriages.
Paul IV against the Unitarians, renewed by Pius IV.
The Tridentine Profession of Faith (1564), required of clergy and teachers.
Pius V on exchanges of money.
The profession of faith prescribed by Gregory XIII for the Greeks.
Clement VIII on priests blessing oils and on ordinations of schismatics.
Clement VIII condemns sacramental confession and absolution by letter or messenger.
Paul V ends the controversy on grace: Thomists and Molinists may each teach their view, and neither may call the other heretical.
Innocent X condemns as heretical the claim that Peter and Paul are two equal heads of the Church.
Innocent X on the controversy over grace.
The formulary of submission required of Jansenists.
Alexander VII's Sollicitudo (1661) on the Immaculate Conception, forbidding attacks on the belief.
Alexander VII condemns 45 propositions of moral laxism.
Alexander VII forbids each side in the dispute over imperfect contrition to censure the other.
Innocent XI on frequent and daily Communion.
Innocent XI condemns 65 propositions of moral laxism and errors on 'donated omnipotence'.
Innocent XI permits defending probabiliorism against probabilism.
Innocent XI condemns using knowledge from confession to the penitent's harm.
Alexander VIII condemns the doctrine of 'philosophical sin'.
Alexander VIII condemns 31 Jansenist propositions.
Holy Office replies (1703) on what an adult must explicitly believe before baptism.
Clement XI's Vineam Domini: respectful silence does not satisfy the obedience due to the condemnation of Jansen's sense.
Benedict XIV's declaration on clandestine and mixed marriages in Belgium and Holland.
Benedict XIV on priests as extraordinary ministers of confirmation in the East.
The profession of faith prescribed for the Maronites and other Orientals.
Benedict XIV forbids confessors to demand the name of an accomplice.
Benedict XIV on the baptism of Jewish children, rules of their time.
Benedict XIV condemns propositions excusing duelling.
Pius VI on mixed marriages, and on the Church's power over the marriages of the baptized.
Pius VII on the indissolubility of marriage.
Pius VII and Leo XII on vernacular versions of Scripture without approved notes.
Replies of Pius VIII and the Holy Office: penitents taking moderate legal interest are not to be disturbed while the question is pending.
Gregory XVI's Mirari vos (1832) against indifferentism and Lamennais's views.
Gregory XVI's Singulari nos condemns Lamennais's Paroles d'un croyant.
Gregory XVI condemns the works of Georg Hermes.
Propositions Louis Bautain was required to sign, against fideism.
Gregory XVI on the matter of anointing and on Bible societies.
Pius IX's Qui pluribus on faith and reason, and on civil marriage.
Pius IX's Singulari quadam (1854) on rationalism, indifferentism and invincible ignorance.
Propositions Augustin Bonnetty was required to sign, against traditionalism.
The Holy Office on the misuse of magnetism (1856).
Pius IX against Anton Günther, and the Holy Office against the ontologists.
Pius IX's Gravissimas inter against Frohschammer on the freedom of science.
Pius IX's Quanto conficiamur (1863) on indifferentism and invincible ignorance.
Pius IX's Tuas libenter on the ordinary magisterium, and the Holy Office against the branch theory of the Church.
The index of the documents from which the Syllabus is drawn.
The closing exhortations of Dei Filius.
Pius IX on the two powers and the freedom of the Church in Prussia.
The Holy Office rejects a proposed explanation of transubstantiation as intolerable (1875).
Pius IX on royal assent to papal acts.
Leo XIII and the Holy Office on receiving converts, socialism, marriage, political power, secret societies and assistance at duels.
The Holy Office's prohibition of cremation (1886), a discipline relaxed in 1963 while the Church still prefers burial.
Leo XIII on civil divorce and Immortale Dei on the Christian constitution of states.
Holy Office replies: it cannot be safely taught that craniotomy or any operation directly killing the fetus or the mother is lawful.
The closing of the Rosmini decree.
Leo XIII's encyclicals on liberty, the laity, the Eucharist, Rerum Novarum and Mary as Mediatrix.
Leo XIII's Providentissimus Deus on the study of Scripture and its inerrancy.
Leo XIII's Satis cognitum on the unity of the Church.
The Holy Office on the faith and intention required for baptism.
Leo XIII's Testem benevolentiae: the opinions called Americanism, condemned in the sense described.
Leo XIII on the matter of baptism and on the Eucharist.
Pius X's Ad diem illum: Mary as dispenser of graces.
Biblical Commission replies on implicit citations and on historical narratives in Scripture.
Pius X's decree on frequent and daily Communion.
Pius X's Ne temere on the form of marriage, and on mixed marriages in Germany.
Pius X's Vehementer nos against the separation of Church and state in France.
The short form of anointing in urgent cases.
Biblical Commission replies on the Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch.
The closing of Lamentabili.
Ne temere on betrothal and marriage.
Pius X's Pascendi on the doctrines of the Modernists.
Biblical Commission replies on the Fourth Gospel.
Pius X's Praestantia Scripturae: obedience to the Biblical Commission's decisions is required, with penalties.
Biblical Commission replies on Isaiah.
Pius X on the relation of philosophy and theology.
Biblical Commission replies on Genesis 1–3 and on the Psalms.
Pius X's Quam singulari on the age for first Communion.
Pius X condemns certain errors of the Orientals.
Biblical Commission replies on the Gospels, Acts, the Pastoral Epistles, Hebrews and the Parousia.
The Holy Office on absolving dying schismatics in good faith.
Benedict XV and the Holy Office on spiritism, Christ's knowledge, inerrancy (Spiritus Paraclitus) and theosophy.
Pius XI on Church and state, St. Thomas, the revival of merits, the kingship of Christ and laicism.
The Holy Office on the Johannine Comma (1897), clarified in 1927 to allow scholars to investigate it.
The Holy Office forbids Catholics to take part in non-Catholic unity conferences (1927), a discipline later changed.
Pius XI on the liturgy, education (Divini illius magistri) and Christian marriage (Casti Connubii).
Pius XI and the Holy Office on abortion, sterilization, the family, social order (Quadragesimo Anno) and Mary's motherhood.
Biblical Commission reply against two misinterpretations of Scripture.
Pius XI and Pius XII on the priesthood, social justice, the natural law, the Mystical Body, Scripture (Divino afflante), marriage and the liturgy (Mediator Dei).
Pius XII's Sacramentum ordinis (1947), deciding with supreme authority the matter and form of holy orders.
The Biblical Commission's letter to Cardinal Suhard on the Pentateuch.
Pius XII on artificial fertilization and the Holy Office on the intention in baptism.
Pius XII's Humani generis on errors threatening the foundations of doctrine.
The opening of Munificentissimus Deus; the definition follows (n. 2333).
Boniface I on the primacy (appendix).
The Formula of Union (433) between Cyril and the Antiochenes, approved by Sixtus III.
Urban IV on the Eucharistic feast, and Holy Office replies on impurity and marriage.

Adopted while three men claimed the papacy and the claimant who had convoked the council, John XXIII, had fled. No pope confirmed it as such: Martin V approved what the council decided conciliariter in matters of faith, and Eugene IV accepted Constance only without prejudice to the rights, dignity and pre-eminence of the Apostolic See. Vatican I's definitions on the primacy exclude the conciliarist reading. Whether it was a dogmatic claim, an emergency measure for a schism, or a legal decree is still argued.

Juridical acts that ended the schism. Many historians and canonists date the council's ecumenical standing from Gregory XII's convocation in session 14, which is one reason the earlier sessions, including Haec Sancta, are judged differently.
A disciplinary law on the frequency of councils. It was followed once (Pavia–Siena 1423–1424, then Basel 1431) and then lapsed; later popes did not treat it as binding.
Disciplinary and constitutional measures. The profession of faith is in line with the older papal professions; the rest lapsed with Frequens.
Measures for the election that ended the schism. The reform points were taken up in session 43 and in concordats with the nations.

A juridical act of Martin V, promulgated in the council after his election. In his own words the deposition of session 12 (C2) was "canonical" and "from the papacy" by "definitive sentence." It shows how Martin regarded the council's acts against the claimants; by itself it says nothing about Haec Sancta (C1).
Disciplinary reform, approved by Martin V.

The text on which every later judgment of Constance turns. The approval is limited twice: to matters of faith, and to what was done conciliariter. Most Catholic theologians hold that Haec Sancta, passed when the assembly was not yet undisputedly a general council, falls outside it; conciliarists hold that it was a decree on faith passed in full session. The occasion was the Falkenberg case, which the council had treated in committee rather than in session.
The papal acts that decided how far Constance's decrees bind. The documents follow this summary.

Chancery usage of Martin V himself: the Pisan pope Alexander V is "our predecessor," John XXIII "succeeded him in the papacy," and Martin was elected after John's deposition "from the papacy." The Annuario Pontificio now lists both Pisan popes as antipopes, and Angelo Roncalli took the name John XXIII in 1958. See the disputed question on the Pisan popes.
Martin V protects the acts that ended the schism (the depositions and his own election) from review by the next council. It is a papal act about Constance, not a conciliar decree.

The appeal was the Polish appeal to a future council in the Falkenberg affair (see C9). Martin V had rejected such appeals in consistory on 10 March 1418; here he praises the king for holding that there is no appeal from the pope, the principle later fixed by Pius II (n. 717).

Written against Alfonso's support for the Luna party. Martin V calls Constance a general council that "represented the universal Church" and treats its sentence against Benedict XIII (session 37) as due process.

The synod met as the last remnant of the Avignon obedience in Aragon came to an end, with the abdication of Gil Sánchez Muñoz ("Clement VIII") that year. Under a papal legate it calls Constance a general council "gathered in the Holy Spirit." Its wording is careful on the old question of legitimacy: John XXIII and Benedict XIII lost whatever right "they claimed to have," and Gregory XII renounced "whatever right belonged to him," without saying which of them was pope.
Martin V says he has altered nothing in the reform decrees published at Constance (see C6).
Enacted against an express papal dissolution. Its force depends on how one judges Haec Sancta and Eugene IV's later recognition of the council.

Conciliarists read it as papal approval of Basel and its claims. Others note that it recognized the council's legitimacy without ratifying its decrees or accepting its supremacy, and that the pope later reserved the rights of the Apostolic See.
Repeats the claim of session 2.

A disciplinary concession that kept the doctrine defined at Constance (n. 626) and later at Trent (n. 930–937): Communion under one kind is complete, and the chalice for the laity is a matter of the Church's discipline.
Disciplinary measures of their time. The Church's later teaching rejects contempt for the Jewish people and every form of antisemitism (Nostra Aetate 4).

Reform law. Some of it, such as the rule on shunning excommunicates, matched what Martin V had already granted; much of it entered national settlements such as the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges (1438), which Lateran V later annulled (n. 740).
Most Catholic historians treat Basel as without authority from the transfer onward; Lateran V gives this as the reason its later acts have no weight (n. 740).
Enacted after the transfer, and condemned by the Council of Florence in Moyses vir Dei as contrary to Scripture, the Fathers and the true sense of Constance.
Acts of a schismatic assembly, annulled by Florence. Felix V is counted an antipope.
Without authority, because enacted by the assembly after the transfer; Sixtus IV still allowed both opinions (n. 734–735). The doctrine itself was defined by Pius IX in 1854 (n. 1641).
A decree of the ecumenical Council of Florence, Denzinger's era n. 691–715.
Two limits are written into the reception: Basel only up to its transfer (B7), and nothing against the rights of the Apostolic See and the power given to Peter and his successor.

The strongest papal language about Constance. It receives the council "as all other councils" and as its predecessors did, so it adds nothing beyond what earlier popes had approved; read with B13 and with the protest issued the same day (B15). Conciliarists read it as acceptance of Constance's claims on councils; others as a concession of form, limited by the reservation.
This is why historians call the 1447 settlement clouded: the concessions (B14) and the reservation were issued together. Summary only; check the text in Mercati before citing.

Whether it names Ad ea ex debito, or the reservation (B15), has still to be read in Mercati. Nicholas V then concluded the Concordat of Vienna (1448), confirmed by the bull Ad sacram Petri sedem of 19 March 1448.
The settlement that closed the conciliar crisis.

How the papal side read Haec Sancta after Basel, from the man who as Pius II forbade appeals to a council in 1460 (n. 717) and in 1463 retracted his own Basel-era conciliarism in In minoribus agentes (B18). He limits the decree to a pope who is not certain or has ceased to be pope: the old canonists' exception for heresy (Gratian, D. 40 c. 6, "unless he is found to have strayed from the faith"), widened to grave scandal to the whole Church. That second case is his own reading; later teaching holds that the First See is judged by no one (Vatican I, n. 1830; canon 1404 of the 1983 Code).

Pius II retracts the conciliarism of his Basel years and states his settled view as pope, three years after Execrabilis (n. 717). In one passage he both recognizes the authority of a general council "as it was declared and defined" at Constance and says no approved council met without papal authority while there was an unquestioned pope. Read together with his 1452 oration (B17): what Constance declared holds for a Church whose head was in doubt, and does not set a council over a certain pope.

A penal decree protecting the council until the election, passed at the session in which Gregory XII's representative convoked the council and his resignation was received (C2). Some read its sanction on whoever violates the council's statutes as covering Haec Sancta; others note that it is a disciplinary measure for the council's duration, and that a penal law does not define doctrine.

In his own words Eugene IV yielded to the council and assented to its decree "as you dictated," having differed only over the place. Conciliarists read this as acceptance of Basel's earlier sessions, including the renewal of Haec Sancta (B1). Others read the yielding as about the council's continuation, which is what Dudum sacrum declared (B2), and point to his later transfer of the council (B7), Moyses vir Dei (B11) and his reservation of 1447 (B15).
